clue.text: Pull something off to discover rabbit, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: to succeed, to achieve what was wanted
second meaning: what a conjuror does when a rabbit appears from the hat

explanation.surface: A conjuror succeeds in revealing a rabbit from a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means to work or succeed, and literally describes performing a magic illusion such as producing a rabbit.

clue.text: Girl's day of birth? Just the opposite

definitions.text: day of birth? Just the opposite

blocks.note: first meaning: a woman's first name

blocks.clueFragment: day of birth? Just the opposite
blocks.note: second meaning: swap the words round to get the birth of a day, which is daybreak

explanation.surface: Asking about a young woman's birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just the opposite' tells you to turn 'day of birth' round into 'birth of day'.
explanation.definitionFit: Daybreak is when each new day begins, its birth, and the word is also a common female first name.

clue.text: Rear of plane turned in flight

blocks.note: first meaning: the back section of an aircraft
second meaning: to turn this is to run away, so it is what gets turned when fleeing

explanation.surface: The back of an aircraft swings round while it is flying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' looks like air travel, but here it means fleeing: to turn tail is to run away.
explanation.definitionFit: The rearmost part of an aircraft carries this name, and the idiom 'turn tail' means to retreat or bolt.

clue.text: Factors, perhaps, involved in home affairs

definitions.text: Factors, perhaps, involved in home affairs

blocks.clueFragment: Factors, perhaps, involved in home affairs
blocks.note: surface reading: elements that play a part in domestic or national business

blocks.clueFragment: Factors, perhaps, involved in home affairs
blocks.note: setter's reading: people who act for others in buying and selling houses; factor is the Scottish word for a property manager

explanation.surface: Considerations that bear on domestic matters, or on the Home Office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Factors' reads as influences, but a factor is also an agent who manages property, especially in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Property agents handle the sale and letting of houses, so their whole business is home affairs.

clue.text: Arrest Pole in bankruptcy case

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, surrounded

blocks.note: north pole, abbreviated N
bankruptcy is financial ruin; 'case' is the outer piece that holds the other

explanation.surface: A Polish man is detained in connection with a bankruptcy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' suggests a Polish person, but in crosswords it is usually a magnetic pole, N or S.
explanation.definitionFit: To run someone in is an informal phrasal verb for taking them into custody, the same as an arrest.

clue.text: Where you might get ice after a stew

definitions.text: Where you might get ice after a stew

indicators.note: a stew is a jumble of ingredients cooked together, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A canteen where you could have ice cream after your stew.
explanation.walkthrough: This is close to an &lit: the whole clue is the definition, while 'stew' doubles as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-service restaurant is a place serving a main course followed by an ice-cream dessert.

clue.text: Hebridean section - an ocean, you might say

definitions.note: said aloud, these words sound like 'a notion'

indicators.note: a section is a part cut from a whole, so the letters sit inside the word

blocks.note: the middle letters of this word

explanation.surface: A stretch of Hebridean sea described as a whole ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is spoken: 'an ocean' run together sounds like 'a notion'. The Hebrides are islands off the west coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A notion is a thought or concept formed in the mind, a direct synonym.

clue.text: News of the French plots

blocks.note: French for 'of the' with a plural noun
a plot of land is a patch

explanation.surface: Reports about schemes being hatched in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plots' suggests conspiracies, but it means small pieces of ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Dispatches are official reports sent from the front or abroad, a form of news.

clue.text: As immature as such lack of expertise could be

definitions.text: As immature as such lack of expertise could be

blocks.clueFragment: As immature as such lack of expertise could be
blocks.note: surface reading: inexperience can make work look childish

blocks.clueFragment: As immature as such lack of expertise could be
blocks.note: setter's reading: the adjective for work done by an unskilled non-professional

explanation.surface: A remark that lack of skill can look as childish as this.
explanation.walkthrough: The word describing an unpaid hobbyist's poor work is meant, not any word for childishness.
explanation.definitionFit: Work that is unskilled and inept, like that of a non-professional, shows a lack of competence.

clue.text: On paper, cricket side given no chance

blocks.note: something on paper has been put down in writing
the off side is one half of a cricket field

explanation.surface: On paper, a cricket team is reckoned to have no hope.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the field is split into the off side and the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: To be written off is to be dismissed as a failure or as having no hope of success.

clue.text: Mount donkey and circle back

indicators.note: going back means reading from right to left

blocks.note: an ass is a donkey
the letter shaped like a circle

explanation.surface: Climb onto a donkey and ride round back home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' looks like a verb, getting on the donkey, but it is a mountain: Ossa is a peak in Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: Ossa is a mountain in Thessaly, Greece, famous in myth for being piled on Pelion.

clue.text: Lay about more savage types in confusion

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: to lay money is to bet it
wilder is more savage, and men are types

explanation.surface: Fiercer people are left baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay' suggests putting down or a song, but it is a wager.
explanation.definitionFit: Bewilderment is a state of being thoroughly puzzled, which is confusion.

clue.text: Put up with the piano one has, to keep up with the others

definitions.text: to keep up with the others

blocks.note: to stand something is to tolerate it
taken as written
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
an ace is a one in cards

explanation.surface: Tolerating the piano a person owns in order to keep up with the neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: In music P stands for piano, meaning quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand the pace is an idiom for matching the speed of rivals without falling behind.

clue.text: West End farce finishes up a vehicle for the stars

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter
in a down entry, up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: the last letter of this word
taken as written
to cap something is to finish it off on top

explanation.surface: A London theatre comedy whose ending turns out to be a hit for its star actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' looks like London's theatre district, but it means the end of the word West.
explanation.definitionFit: A spacecraft carries astronauts towards the stars, a vehicle in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Rattle for little girl's music-making

blocks.note: Di is short for Diana, a girl's name, with the possessive s
a concert is a performance of music

explanation.surface: A baby's rattle for a small girl's musical play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rattle' looks like a baby's toy, but it is a verb, to unsettle.
explanation.definitionFit: To rattle someone is to unnerve or fluster them, which is what disconcert means.

clue.text: Court habitually sees little boy with king

blocks.note: Phil is short for Philip
and means together with
Edwardus Rex, a king's royal cipher

explanation.surface: A royal court watches a small boy who is with the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' looks like a noun, a royal or legal court, but it is a verb, to woo.
explanation.definitionFit: To philander is to flirt or have casual affairs with many women, wooing as a habit.

clue.text: Move fast to get on target in game

blocks.note: to dart is to dash quickly
to board a bus or ship is to get on it

explanation.surface: Hurrying to stay on course in a game.
explanation.definitionFit: The circular board that players throw small arrows at in the pub game is their target.

clue.text: Provoke today's top dog?

blocks.note: what is in is fashionable at present
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: Asking whether the current top dog is a provocation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top dog' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'today's top' is the fashionable thing, then a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur trouble or anger is to bring it on yourself, to provoke it.

clue.text: Progress by one's own efforts in revolutionary movement

blocks.note: first meaning: to travel by pedalling a bicycle
second meaning: a motion that goes round and returns to its start

explanation.surface: Getting ahead through hard work within a political uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests politics, but it means turning in circles.
explanation.definitionFit: Riding a bike moves you along under your own pedal power, and a repeating round of events is a recurring circuit.

clue.text: Soldiers given direction to prepare for another posting

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
the directions on a letter tell the post office where to send it

explanation.surface: Troops receive orders before being sent to a new station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posting' looks like a military transfer, but it is sending mail.
explanation.definitionFit: To readdress a letter is to write a new destination on it so it can be sent on again.

clue.text: Such a lot of unhappiness, according to the sergeant

definitions.text: Such a lot of unhappiness, according to the sergeant

blocks.clueFragment: Such a lot of unhappiness, according to the sergeant
blocks.note: surface reading: an army sergeant complaining about how miserable everything is

blocks.clueFragment: Such a lot of unhappiness, according to the sergeant
blocks.note: setter's reading: the police sergeant in The Pirates of Penzance sings that a policeman's lot is not a happy one

explanation.surface: A sergeant grumbling about the misery of the job.
explanation.walkthrough: The sergeant is the police one in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera, whose song begins 'When constabulary duty's to be done'.
explanation.definitionFit: A police force as a body is made up of officers whose lot, says the song, is not a happy one.

clue.text: Flexible one, for a change, in lathe

indicators.note: a change means one letter is swapped out and another put in its place

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written, a turning machine

explanation.surface: A supple piece is swapped into a lathe.
explanation.walkthrough: The I replaces the A of the machine's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithe means supple and bending easily, so it describes a flexible body.

clue.text: Audibly disapprove of ring-leader, a nasty type

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so take the opening letter

blocks.note: to boo is to jeer out loud
the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: Loudly criticising the chief of a gang, an unpleasant person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring-leader' reads as one word, but it splits: the leader of the word ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A boor is a rude, coarse, ill-mannered person, an unpleasant character.

clue.text: Brook or river

blocks.note: first meaning: to put up with
second meaning: a river in north-east England flowing through Durham

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brook' looks like a stream to go with 'river', but it is a verb meaning tolerate.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, to wear something is to accept or tolerate it; the Wear is a river in County Durham, England.

clue.text: Top copy? Times finally appears

blocks.note: to ape is to imitate
the multiplication sign

explanation.surface: A top copy of The Times newspaper finally comes out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like this newspaper, but it is the sign for multiplying.
explanation.definitionFit: The apex is the highest point or peak of something, its top.

clue.text: Old game that's fought over, as you might say

indicators.note: the words are to be pronounced, not spelt

blocks.note: fought is battled, and o'er is the poetic form of over

explanation.surface: An old pastime that people struggled over.
explanation.walkthrough: O'er is the old poetic contraction of over.
explanation.definitionFit: Battledore and shuttlecock was an early form of badminton, an old game played with a small racket.

clue.text: Bear giving better chance

blocks.note: first meaning: to carry
second meaning: the betting system at racecourses that gives a punter a chance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like an adjective, but it is a person who bets.
explanation.definitionFit: To tote is to carry, and the tote is the pool betting system at British race meetings, offering odds to punters.

clue.text: Foolishly underrate holding against gambler

indicators.note: acting foolishly is acting in a muddled way, so the letters are jumbled
holding means having something gripped inside

blocks.note: taken as written
v is short for versus, against

explanation.surface: Unwisely dismissing opposition to a risk-taker.
explanation.definitionFit: An adventurer is someone who takes risks for gain, a speculator or chancer.
